707110.t: Ultimately from Proto-West Semitic *gamal-; compare Arabic جَمَل (jamal) and Hebrew גָּמָל (gāmā́l), Proto-Nakh *imkal, Old Georgian აქლემი (aklemi) and Tocharian A oṅkaläm (“elephant”).

707169.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kərpós or *karpós, from Proto-Indo-European *kerp- (“pluck, harvest”), though debated whether via inheritance or borrowing from a different Indo-European branch due to the problematic α (a) in the Greek form.

707118.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kámptō, *kamptos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂emp- (“to bend, curve”), possibly related to Latin campus and Lithuanian kampas, kumpas.

707109.t: From κάμηλος (kắmēlos, “camel”) + πάρδαλις (pắrdălĭs, “leopard”); from the fact that a giraffe has a long neck like a camel and is spotted like a leopard.

707187.t: Of unclear origin. Traditionally compared with Latin carīna (“ship's keel; shell of a nut”) and Sanskrit करक (karaka, “water jar; coconut (shell)”).

707132.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kapnós, from Proto-Indo-European *kwep- (“to smoke, boil, move violently”), which appears to be a European substrate word; see also Lithuanian kūpėti (“to boil over”), Old Church Slavonic кꙑпѣти (kypěti, “to boil”), Sanskrit कुप्यति…

707126.t: Uncertain, sometimes suggested to be related to Proto-Slavic *kǫtъ (“corner”), Proto-Celtic *kantos (“corner, rim (of a chariot wheel)”) through a Proto-Indo-European *kh₂ndʰ-, but Beekes doesn't find this convincing, as -νθ- (-nth-) is often indicative of…

707198.t: An Elamite origin has been suggested but, according to Beekes, the group σσ/ττ (ss/tt) is typically Pre-Greek, so the word would have come from Greece or Western Anatolia, like μόλυβδος (mólubdos, “lead”), but even if so, the word might still go back to…

707128.t: Likely Pre-Greek, and generally connected with κάννα (kánna, “reed”).

707108.t: Possibly an Old Iranian borrowing, from Proto-Iranian *kamarā- (“something curved”), from *kamárati, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *kmárati, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂em- (“to bend, curve”).

707102.t: Uncertain. The etymology determination is complicated by the fact that the word is similar to Ancient Greek κρύπτω (krŭ́ptō, “to hide; cover”) in form and sense, thus indicating possible (bi-directional) analogical influence.

707167.t: From καρπός (kărpós, “fruit”) + -ιμος (-ĭmos, suffix for adjective of capability).

707136.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kapt͏̌ō, from Proto-Indo-European *kap-yé-ti, from *kap- (“seize, grab”). Exact cognate of Latin capiō, (English have).

707100.t: Perhaps related to καλύπτω (kalúptō, “to cover”), despite the difference in the final consonant. The expected form would be *κάλυψ (*kálups).

707165.t: κάρπασος (kárpăsos) [from the Hebrew כַּרְפַּס (karpás, “a type of expensive fabric made of cotton”)] + -ινος (-inos)

707117.t: Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *kampā́, from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂emp-, from *kh₂em- (“to bend, curve”). By surface analysis, κάμπτω (kámptō, “to bend”) + -ή (-ḗ).

707114.t: From κατα- (kata-, “down”) + μύω (múō, “to close, to shut”).

707189.t: From κάρφω (kárphō, “to dry up, to wither”) + -ος (-os). Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐂓 (ka+po).

707177.t: Uncertain. * Maybe from Proto-Indo-European *k(e)rt- (“to turn”), related to Ancient Greek κυρτία (kurtía, “anything made of wicker”), Sanskrit कृणत्ति (kṛṇátti, “to twist thread, to spin”), Sanskrit चृटति (cṛṭáti, “to bind, to fasten together”), Latin…

707129.t: Beekes finds improbable a derivation from κάπη (kápē, “crib, manger”). Probably related to Latin caupō (“innkeeper”); as the Greek could be from Pre-Greek, this would render the Latin a substrate borrowing, as well.

707135.t: The word has been connected with Persian کبر (kabar, “caper”) and Burushaski [script needed] (čopuri) (a language isolate), suggesting an Oriental origin.

707194.t: From a Semitic source equalling Hebrew קְצִיעָה (qəṣīʿā), Aramaic קְצִיעֲתָא (qəṣīʿătā), from קְצַע (qṣaʿ, “to cut off”), referencing the manner the tree produce is reaped.

707113.t: A technical loan of unknown origin. The comparison with καμάρα (kamára, “vaulted chamber”) has little value, while the one with Proto-Slavic *kamy (“stone”) is possible.

707125.t: Uncertain. * The origin of the beetle-name is unclear, but it may be an r-stem-suffixation to κάνθων (kánthōn, “pack-ass”) as suggested by Strömberg, since the scarab is recognized for and likened by his transporting packs of dung.

707164.t: From κάρος (kắros, “heavy sleep, torpor”) + -όω (-óō, verbal suffix).
